III. THE FRENCH CONNECTION (1 of 2 post)

Our situation is similar to that of the French between 1789-1799. Andrew D. White, American scholar, author, and diplomat addressed members of Congress in 1876 during the greenback craze on "Fiat Money Inflation in France--How It came,What It Brought and How It Ended." White observed:

Every other attempt of the same kind in human history, [the attempt to use fiat money] under whatever circumstances, has reached similar results in kind if not in degree; all of them show the existence of financial laws as real in their operation as those which hold the planets in their courses.

The laws of finance, like all natural laws, are impersonal. They operate without favoritism. They came into play during the French Revolution with a vengeance primarily because the French people had not learned from their own history.

Around 1720, under the influence of John Law, the French government had decreed the issuance of a money-substitute and made it legal tender, with no secure backing or promise of redemption. The results were disastrous

When Louis XVI and his queen, Marie Antoinette, ascended to the throne in 1774, the king and his government went deep into debt and discredit. They called together a parliament, the Estates-General, which had not met for 174 years, to raise revenue. Throughout France, there came a plea for the issuance of a money substitute as a shortcut to prosperity. Some warned of the pitfalls of a money substitute system.

Those in favor argued that France was the one nation that could safely issue a money-substitute. Unlike the days when a money-substitute was issued during the reign of an absolute monarchy dominated by politicians and adventurers. France was now a constitutional government controlled by an enlightened, patriotic people. France would be able to secure every livre of her money-substitute with a mortgage on land With such able men in the government, France would not make the same mistakes it had under John Law.

In April 1790, the National Assembly decreed the first issuance of paper currency in the form of assignats, notes which would bear interest to the holder at three percent. They began depreciating almost immediately. Despite several more issues, by the end of September 1790, hard times had come again.

A pamphlet representing the minority view of the National Assembly warned:

... doubling the quantity of money or substitutes for money in a nation simply increases prices, disturbs values, alarms capital, diminishes legitimate enterprise, and so decreases the demand both for products and for labor; that the only persons to be helped by it are the rich who have large debts to pay.

As the government issued more and more paper, prices rose. Gold, silver, and copper money began to disappear, and confusion and fraud spread. To keep silver and copper in circulation, the law required citizens to send their silverware and jewelry to be melted down. Even church bells were melted down for copper. These measures proved futile.

To quote Andrew White:

... in issues of irredeemable currency, in obedience to the theories of a legislative body or of the people at large, there is a natural law of rapidly increasing emission and depreciation. [i]

The doctrine that developed in France at this time is one that has cropped up periodically throughout history: that all currency is efficient because of the official stamp it bears, and that government may pay its debts and become prosperous simply by use of a printing press. This is the basis of our money-substitute system today.

The French blamed every cause but the right one. They blamed speculators, brokers, businessmen, the Bourbon family, British agents, imports being greater than exports. As a remedy, the authorities seized hoarded specie from citizens, and considered punishing hoarders with the death penalty.

The disappearance of specie was the result of a simple, inevitable natural law. The superior currency was falling out of circulation because of the use of an inferior one. Hoarding was not an act of unpatriotic madness, but the inevitable result of the paper currency system.

After each new issue, there was a marked depreciation of the currency. As the quantity of paper currency in circulation increased, it first stimulated production. But soon markets were so glutted that the demand for goods diminished. "One manufactory after another stopped," thousands of workmen were discharged, and "heavy duties were put upon foreign goods. …" Commerce became spasmodic, business grew stagnant, and trade diminished. Capitalists were afraid to invest in business, and merchants had to charge enough to ensure that their profit would cover probable fluctuations in value. As a result, prices rose even more sharply. At the same time, wages dropped because so many workmen were unemployed.

The French, a naturally thrifty people, lost all desire to save or practice thrift. Likewise, there came an increase in speculation and gambling. There grew a dislike of steady labor and a contempt for moderate gains and simple living. As the producing classes became poorer, businesses could not employ as many workmen. Here was a classic example of Daniel Webster's observation that "of all the contrivances for cheating the laboring classes of mankind, none has been more effective than that which deludes them with paper-money." Bribery of legislators became a matter of course. Corruption in high places caused public distrust, cynicism, and lack of patriotism.

The French irredeemable, paper currency experiment saw the growth of a vast debtor class who came to realize that the depreciated currency worked in its favor. Since a devalued currency would enable them to pay their debts with money of less value, debtors demanded new issues of paper. And although each new issue made things worse, the people superstitiously believed that the poor could become rich if "enough paper money were issued and were more cunningly handled.”

The Legislative Assembly next suspended payment for all amounts above 10,000 francs owed to public creditors. When hunger continued to press on the French people, the question resounded, Why is food still so dear?" The most widely accepted answer was, "Because Louis is still alive." In mid-January 1792, a majority of the National Convention voted Louis guilty of conspiring against liberty, and sentenced him to death. Marie Antoinette suffered the same fate in mid-October.

In 1793, the government confiscated large estates of those who had emigrated from France. The depreciation of the currency was sometimes masked as the value rose and fell. Overall, prices continued to rise, and commonly used articles became expensive. Paris washerwomen, unable to afford soap for their laundries, demanded that those merchants who refused to sell their goods because they were trying to save property should be put to death. There were calls for a law "to equalize the value of paper money and silver coin." There was a cry for the rich to be taxed in large amounts so that the people could have the money to buy bread, and for hanging shopkeepers and plundering stores."

By 1793, the French economy was faltering dangerously. The government tried a forced loan "levied upon all married men with incomes of 10,000 francs, and upon all unmarried men with incomes of 6,000 francs.° Because so many of the rich had fled the country or hidden their wealth, only 1/5 of the required sum could be raised. Therefore, a new law levied forced loans on incomes as low as 1,000 francs. Smaller proprietors had to pay 1/10 and larger proprietors with incomes above 9,000 francs 1/2 of their incomes. The government made no provision to repay this loan.

Another expedient was the Law of the Maximum, a form of wage and price control. Everyone tried to evade the fixed prices. Farmers brought as little produce as possible to market. They could not afford to raise crops at the legally required price. But when he held his crops or cattle from market, they were often taken from him by force. Neither could shopkeepers afford to sell their goods at the 1790 price. Many went out of business. Many others forced consumers to pay enormous prices to justify the risk of trading. This was not just an excuse, for people were guillotined daily, many for breaking the Maximum laws.

To find goods that were hidden by farmers and shopkeepers, the people were encouraged to spy on each other for a reward. To force compliance, the Criminal Tribunal at Strassbourg, for instance, was authorized to "destroy the dwelling of any one found guilty of selling goods above the price set by law."

Still, the Law of the Maximum was not succeeding. The National Convention passed more laws. Any person:

Selling gold or silver coin, or making any difference in any transaction

between paper and specie should be imprisoned in irons for six years;

... [refusing] to accept a payment in assignats or accepting assignats

at a discount, [the first time] should pay a fine of three thousand

francs; .. . committing this crime a second time should pay a fine of

six thousand francs and suffer imprisonment twenty years in irons.
